hero.name: Neelam
hero.who: a 41-year-old Hindi teacher in Lucknow who reaches for her phone without thinking

story.b: Neelam teaches Hindi at a girls' school in Aliganj, Lucknow. Her phone is never far away. She checks it while the dal cooks, between classes, at every red light in the auto, and even while her son describes his cricket match. She is in fourteen WhatsApp groups. At night she means to read the novel her sister gifted her, and instead watches recipe reels she will never cook. One Sunday the phone shows her screen time, almost five hours a day. She feels a little sick. Worse, she cannot remember anything she watched yesterday. On Monday she deletes Instagram in a burst of anger. By Wednesday night it is back on her phone.

ask.q: Neelam deleted an app and reinstalled it within two days. Which approach is more likely to last?
o: Delete every app at once and switch to a basic phone
Decide what she truly values, then keep only the tools that serve it
Set strict five-minute timers on each app and try harder
ask.why: Deleting in a rush leaves an empty gap, so the apps creep back. A basic phone is extreme when school and family run on WhatsApp. Timers lean on willpower. Starting from her values gives her a clear reason to choose each tool on purpose.

chapters.take: Choose tools for what you value, not for what they offer.

story.h: The back of an answer sheet
story.b: One evening, Neelam takes a spare answer sheet and writes what she truly values. Her son and husband. Teaching well. Reading. Staying close to her mother in Kanpur. The singing she gave up after college. Then she goes through her phone, app by app, and asks a hard question of each one. WhatsApp stays, because school and her mother need it, but she leaves eleven groups. Video calling stays. The shopping app stays, with alerts off. The reels app makes her laugh sometimes, but it serves nothing on her list. Seeing it next to her mother's name on the page, Neelam finds the choice suddenly easy. It is not about giving things up. It is about choosing.

ask.q: Neelam enjoys a reels app now and then. Which question should decide if it stays?
o: Does it give her any benefit at all, even a small one?
Do most of her colleagues use it too?
Is it the best way to support something she truly values?
ask.why: Almost every app offers some small benefit, so that test lets everything in. What colleagues use says nothing about her own life. Asking whether it is the best way to serve a real value is a tougher filter, and it leaves her with fewer, better tools.

chapters.take: Keep the few tools that truly serve your life, and skip the rest.

story.b: With the summer holidays starting, Neelam tries a reset. For one month she removes reels, YouTube and games from her phone. She keeps calls, maps, banking and her three WhatsApp groups. She tells her family she will call instead of forwarding. The first week is strange. Her thumb reaches for the missing apps in the auto, in the bank queue, in bed. Then the gap starts filling. She walks in the colony park in the evenings. She finishes the novel and starts another. She sorts her old music notebooks. At the end of the month she sits down to decide what comes back. YouTube returns, but only on the laptop, only for lesson videos, only on Sundays.

ask.q: The month is over and Neelam misses YouTube a little. What should she do now?
o: Bring it back only if it earns its place, with firm rules
Reinstall everything, since the month proved she can control herself
Never reinstall anything, because missing it means she is addicted
ask.why: The month is a careful reset, not a test of strength. Reinstalling everything throws away what she learned. Refusing everything ignores real uses, like lesson videos for class. Bringing back only what clearly earns its place, with clear rules, keeps the gains.

chapters.take: Clear it all out, then let back in only what earns its place.

story.h: The walk to the sabzi market
story.b: Neelam starts to notice that every small gap in her day used to be filled. The bank queue, the auto ride, even the minutes waiting for the pressure cooker whistle. Now some of those gaps are empty, and at first she does not like it. One evening she walks to the sabzi market without earphones. Halfway there, a feeling she has been avoiding comes up. She is hurt that the principal chose someone else as Class 10 coordinator. On the walk back, carrying tomatoes and methi, she thinks it through calmly. She decides to ask the principal what she could do better next year. At home she feels lighter, as if she has finally heard herself.

ask.q: Her colleague Shabnam says walking without earphones sounds boring. What should Neelam suggest?
o: Use a podcast, since that is at least better than reels
Fill the walk with phone calls so the time is not wasted
Try a short walk with no input and let her thoughts settle
ask.why: Podcasts and calls are better than reels, but they still fill her mind with other voices. Without some quiet time alone, feelings stay unsorted and thinking stays shallow. A short walk with no input gives the mind room to work things out.

chapters.take: Time alone with your thoughts is not empty. It is where you think.

story.b: Neelam's mother in Kanpur sends good morning pictures every day, and for years Neelam has replied with a thumbs up. Her college friend posts photos from her new job in Bengaluru, and Neelam leaves a heart. It all feels like staying in touch. But she realises she has not heard her mother's voice in two weeks. So she starts calling her mother at seven every evening, just for ten minutes, while the rice cooks. Her mother tells her about the neighbour's wedding, the price of mangoes, and a story from her own school days that Neelam has never heard. One Sunday Neelam takes the morning train to Kanpur. They eat kachori together and talk until it is time to leave.

ask.q: Neelam's school friend has just posted photos from a new job. What should Neelam do?
o: Call her that evening and hear about the new job properly
Leave a heart and a long comment so her friend feels noticed
Forward the post to their old school group with congratulations
ask.why: A heart or a comment feels like connection, but it is thin and costs almost nothing. Forwarding the post moves even further from her friend. A call, with a real voice and real questions, actually builds the friendship, and her friend will remember it.

chapters.take: A real conversation beats a hundred little taps on a screen.

story.b: Without the reels, some evenings feel long and empty, and Neelam catches herself drifting towards the TV remote. She remembers that she used to sing at her college programmes, until work and marriage pushed it aside. Her old harmonium sits under a sheet in the store room. She has it tuned at a shop in Aminabad and joins a Saturday evening class for adults near her colony. She practises twenty minutes after dinner, badly at first. Her fingers forget. Her son laughs, then starts tapping the rhythm on the dining table. After practice she feels tired in a good way, the opposite of the heavy tiredness she used to feel after an hour of scrolling.

ask.q: Her evenings feel empty without scrolling. What is the best way for Neelam to fill them?
o: Watch TV serials instead, since at least they are not on the phone
Pick up something hands-on that takes effort, like learning music again
Allow thirty minutes of reels as a reward after a good day
ask.why: If the gap stays empty, the old habit creeps back. TV serials only swap one screen for another, and a reels reward keeps the habit alive. Leisure that takes effort, like music, gives real satisfaction and leaves her more refreshed.

chapters.take: Fill freed time with something real, or the scrolling returns.

story.b: By the end of the term, Neelam's phone still sits on the dining table, but it no longer pulls at her the way it did. She is in three WhatsApp groups. YouTube lives on the laptop for Sunday lesson planning. She walks to the market without earphones and calls her mother at seven. The pile of novels beside her bed has grown, and she is halfway through the third one. On Saturday evenings she goes to her music class, and her son has asked her to teach him the song she practises. Her screen time is something she rarely checks now. When she does, she does not feel sick. She just smiles and puts the phone back down.

chapters.take: Use a few tools on purpose, and give the rest of your life room.
